title: A psalm for each day
hookLine: each weekday has its own psalm, once sung by the Levites in the Temple

cards: Some people have a song for Monday mornings. Some families have Friday pizza, or Sunday pancakes. Giving a day its own flavor keeps the week from turning into one long gray blur.

Jewish prayer does it with music: every day of the week has its own psalm. Near the end of the morning service, someone announces, almost like a radio host: today is the second day of the week. And then comes the song.

teach.h: THE LEVITES' SONGS IN THE TEMPLE.
teach.b: The custom comes from the Temple in Jerusalem. The Mishnah, in tractate Tamid, lists the psalm the Levites sang each day as the daily offering was made.
Sunday, Psalm twenty-four. Monday, forty-eight. Tuesday, eighty-two.
Wednesday, ninety-four. Thursday, eighty-one. Friday, ninety-three.
And on Shabbat, ninety-two, the psalm that calls itself a song for the Sabbath day. The Temple is long gone, but the songs are still sung.
In the prayer book, each one begins with a line like: today is the first day of the week, on which the Levites used to say in the Temple. Notice something: in Hebrew, the weekdays don't have names.
They have numbers, counting toward Shabbat. Every weekday is a step on the way to the seventh.

The Talmud explains why each psalm fits its day by linking it to the days of creation. On the first day, God made the world and owned it, so Sunday's psalm opens: "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof."
On the sixth day, creation was finished and God reigned over it, so Friday's psalm opens: the Lord reigns, clothed in majesty.
Each day of the week remembers its day of the first week. So an ordinary Tuesday, the tradition says, isn't ordinary. It has its own place in the story of creation, and its own song.

how: Near the end of the morning service, the Song of the Day is introduced with 'today is the first (second, third…) day of the week, on which the Levites used to say in the Temple' and then the day's psalm is recited.

games.q: which day, which psalm — tap the pairs.

s: the daily psalms began as songs the Levites sang in the Temple
the Mishnah in tractate Tamid lists them.
Hebrew weekdays have names like the English ones
they're numbered: first day, second day, counting toward Shabbat.
Sunday's psalm opens: the earth is the LORD'S
on the first day, the Talmud says, God made the world and owned it.

games.q: it's the sixth day of the week, when creation was finished. which psalm would the Levites sing?
o: the Lord reigns, clothed in majesty.
games.why: Friday's psalm is 93: the Lord reigns. the Talmud says on the sixth day God finished His work and reigned over it.

practice: Find today's psalm from the list, and if you can look it up, read the first few lines.
If not, think about which day of creation today remembers: light, sky, land and plants, sun and moon, fish and birds, animals and people, or rest. If you pray, you can say today's psalm.
